title: Stand like an anvil (Ignatius to Polycarp 3)
hookLine: stand firm as an anvil under the hammer
tomorrow: why would a bishop shout "away with the atheists"?

lines: A PRISONER WRITES TO A FRIEND.
cards: The family group chat hasn't stopped since breakfast. Every message lands like a hammer: you should, you never, why can't you.
Some weeks the pressure comes exactly like that, blow after blow, and you can feel yourself starting to bend. A man in chains knew the feeling.
Ignatius, the same prisoner from yesterday, is being taken under guard toward Rome. On the way he stops long enough to write to a friend, Polycarp, a bishop with hammers of his own coming.
What do you tell a friend when you may never write to him again?

teach.b: Ignatius doesn't send a pep talk. He sends a picture. First, the hammers.
In chapter three he warns Polycarp about people who seem trustworthy but teach strange things. Don't let them shake you, he says. Second, the anvil.
Stand firm, like an anvil when it's struck. Think about what an anvil does in a blacksmith's shop. It doesn't dodge the hammer, and it doesn't swing back.
It stays, and the hot iron gets shaped on top of it. Third, the athlete.

teach.h: THE ATHLETE TAKES BLOWS AND WINS.
teach.b: Ignatius switches pictures in the same breath: it belongs to a great athlete to take the blows and still win. The win isn't avoiding the hits. It's still standing at the end.
Then he adds the reason: for God's sake we put up with everything, so that God will put up with us. Fourth, where to look.

teach.h: LOOK TO THE ONE ABOVE TIME.
teach.b: Ignatius tells his friend to watch the times, and to wait for the one who is above all time, the unseen one who became visible for our sake.
That's where the steadiness comes from. Not from being hard, but from looking past the hammer.
And the detail to tell a friend tonight: the man who received this letter, Polycarp of Smyrna, would one day need every word of it.

how: Catholics keep feast days for both Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp, and passages from Ignatius's letters are read in the Church's Liturgy of the Hours.

games.q: what does “stand like an anvil” mean?
o: staying steady under blows, without striking back
a blacksmith's rule for keeping the iron hot
a promise never to change your mind about anything

games.q: the letter to Polycarp — tap the pairs.
p: takes the blows and still wins

s: standing firm means hitting back harder than you're hit
Ignatius's anvil never swings. it takes the blow, and the athlete wins by enduring.
the letter is addressed to Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna
Ignatius writes to him by name, as a fellow bishop and friend.
Ignatius tells his friend to keep out of every conflict
he expects blows to come. the point is to stay standing while they land.

games.q: your manager keeps moving your shifts and hinting you're not committed. one coworker says quit, another says blow up at him. what does the anvil do?
o: stay steady: keep doing the work well, and don't take the bait.
quit now, before they can push you out on their terms.
match his pressure with your own until he finally backs off.
games.why: Ignatius's anvil neither dodges nor strikes back. it stays put while the blows land, and for him the steadiness came from looking past the hammer to God.

practice: Stand up, feet flat and a little apart, knees soft, the way an anvil sits on its block. Bring one pressure to mind, just one: a deadline, a person, a voice in your own head.
Let it land, breath after breath, and stay right where you are.

wordCard.voice: Stand like an anvil. Ignatius's advice to a friend under pressure: take the blows without swinging back, and stay.

orig.note: Greek for anvil: Ignatius wrote in Greek, and this is the tool he holds up to Polycarp.

carryVoice: Your line: an anvil. Struck all day, and still there when the hammer stops. See you tomorrow.
